articles.title: China to Tighten Export Controls on Drone Engines, Autopilots and Communication Systems - Мілітарний
articles.summary: China to Tighten Export Controls on Drone Engines, Autopilots and Communication Systems  Мілітарний
articles.full_text:
China will introduce updated export controls on drones and their components from November 18, 2026.
The Ministry of Commerce of the People’s Republic of China (MOFCOM) published the new rules.
They will tighten controls on the export of engines, autopilots, communication equipment, and other components and technologies.
The updated rules introduce export controls on drones with specific flight characteristics. These include aircraft capable of controlled beyond-visual-line-of-sight (BVLOS) flight for between 30 minutes and three hours, provided they can take off and maintain stable flight in wind gusts of 46.3 km/h or higher.
The restrictions will also cover drones capable of flying for at least three hours, as well as certain models with a flight range of 300 km or more.
China will also tighten controls on certain drone components, including specially designed autopilots, certain aircraft engines, onboard radio communication equipment and high-performance brushless electric motors.
For the latter, the rules set technical thresholds including a voltage of 48 V or higher, power output of 3 kW or more, a power-to-weight ratio of at least 3 kW/kg, and a rotational speed of up to 3,000 rpm. The controls will also apply to the corresponding electronic speed controllers and certain carbon-composite propeller blades.
In addition, exporters must provide customs authorities with the technical specifications of the goods, their intended use, and information about the end user. If customs officials doubt the accuracy of a declaration, they can detain the shipment for inspection.
Penalties will apply for the illegal export or resale of products, as well as their use for purposes other than those declared.
MOFCOM said the changes were necessary to protect national security, meet international non-proliferation obligations, and maintain stable global production and supply chains.
China’s new rules could complicate the supply of certain components for Ukrainian and Russian drones, although the actual impact may vary.
For example, Russia could obtain components with the Chinese government’s approval, helping supply amid Russian drone production’s significant dependence on Chinese components.
Meanwhile, for Ukraine, which does not have such close ties with the Chinese government, the new rules could delay the supply of certain components, add inspections, and raise costs.
This mainly affects components that meet the new export controls’ specific criteria, including specialized autopilots, high-power electric motors, electronic speed controllers, communication equipment, and certain types of long-range UAVs.
However, some Chinese products reach Ukraine through intermediaries in Poland, the Czech Republic and other countries.

articles.title: Mexico exports jump 38% as trade deficit returns - upi
articles.summary: Mexico exports jump 38% as trade deficit returns  upi
articles.full_text:
Oct. 27 (UPI) -- Mexico's exports surged 37.9% in September from a year earlier, driven by strong manufacturing and electronics shipments, even as the country recorded a $606 million trade deficit, according to figures released Tuesday by the National Institute of Statistics and Geography.
Exports reached $77.8 billion, the third-highest monthly total on record and the highest for any September, according to Mexican business publication Expansión. Imports climbed 33.1% to $78.4 billion, reversing a $605 million trade surplus recorded in August.
Manufactured goods accounted for most of the growth, with exports rising 39% to $72.8 billion. Shipments of electrical and electronic equipment increased 94.7% from September 2025, while exports of nonautomotive manufactured goods jumped 53%, according to INEGI.
The figures also highlighted Mexico's trade ties with the United States. Non-oil exports to the U.S. market increased 43.5% year over year, compared with a 16.4% rise in shipments to the rest of the world. The Mexican newspaper La Jornada reported that the United States accounted for approximately 84% of Mexico's exports during the first nine months of 2026.
Automotive exports, traditionally one of Mexico's main manufacturing sectors, grew at a slower pace. Shipments rose 5.7% to $16.4 billion, supported by an 8.5% increase in sales to the United States, while exports to other markets declined 7.4%, according to Expansión.
The rapid expansion of electronics exports comes amid growing demand for computers, servers and other equipment used in artificial intelligence infrastructure and data centers. Mexican financial newspaper El Economista identified computing equipment as a major driver of the increase in nonautomotive manufacturing exports.
Despite September's trade deficit, Mexico maintained a cumulative trade surplus of $9.25 billion during the first nine months of 2026, compared with a $3.4 billion deficit during the same period last year, INEGI reported. Total exports reached $627.2 billion, up 30.4%, while imports increased 27.5% to $617.9 billion.
The September deficit reflected a narrowing surplus in non-oil trade, which fell from $4.05 billion in August to $2.75 billion. Mexico's oil trade deficit also declined silghtly, from $3.44 billion to $3.35 billion, according to the statistics agency.

articles.full_text:
By the end of 2026, Ukraine’s trade deficit will exceed $70 billion.
Among the reasons are significant imports of weapons and energy equipment, as well as an increase in purchases of other goods from abroad.
This was stated by Ukraine’s Minister of Economy and Environment, Oleksandr Kravchenko, during the Kyiv International Economic Forum.
According to him, the volume of non-essential imports has risen from $13 billion to $21 billion. To reduce dependence on foreign goods, the government emphasizes the need to support Ukrainian manufacturers and develop the “Made in Ukraine” program.
At the same time, estimates of the deficit vary. The ICU Investment Group forecasts a deficit of $87.4 billion in 2026 and $74.3 billion in 2027. According to the Ministry of Finance’s forecast, the deficit will amount to $69.19 billion this year and rise to $79.66 billion next year.

articles.title: Chinese markets lose trillions as race for AI supremacy with US takes its toll
articles.summary: Lack of profits and the threat posed by western countries are raising concern about the sustainability of Beijing’s AI boomTrillions of dollars have been wiped from China’s stock markets in recent months amid increasing anxiety about the future of artificial intelligence, as Beijing races against the United States for dominance in the sector.The STAR 50 Index, which tracks technology and innovation companies on the Shanghai stock exchange, has plunged 40% since June. articles.full_text:
Trillions of dollars have been wiped from China’s stock markets in recent months amid increasing anxiety about the future of artificial intelligence, as Beijing races against the United States for dominance in the sector.
The STAR 50 Index, which tracks technology and innovation companies on the Shanghai stock exchange, has plunged 40% since June. Other indexes of major companies dropped by about 20% over the same time period.
The precipitous drop has wiped out $2.4tn from the Chinese stock market since May, according to Bloomberg.
AI stocks account for over 40% of the stock market value in China and Hong Kong, according to Goldman Sachs, meaning that any dent in value will send shockwaves across the whole domestic market.
The fall suggests that despite the government’s best efforts to boost China’s technology industries, particularly those which harness the power of AI, the domestic economy does not have the power to sustain a booming market.
The Chinese government has invested heavily into AI, including a 60bn yuan state-backed AI investment fund which started pumping money into domestic developers this month. But Chinese consumers have proved stubbornly reluctant to part with their cash in many parts of the economy – including technology – meaning that many tech companies struggle to turn a profit.
The lack of profits is one of several reasons for the sell-off. Another is the threat of western countries, especially the US, extending bans on Chinese technology.
“This year, the profit margin is not as good as expected. And the US is raising rates. And China’s domestic demand is so weak,” said Dan Wang, the China director for the Eurasia Group. She said that there was a “general anxiety” among technology companies about whether or not the state-backed model would work in the face of weak consumer demand.
The US has banned humanoid robots from China, citing national security risks, and is thought to be considering a ban on Chinese components in data centres. China is heavily reliant on exports and restrictions in the US hurt its domestic companies, which struggle to sell enough products at home.
As China races with the US to pull ahead in AI, Beijing has doubled down on robotics – also known as embodied AI – as the key to rolling out the technology across society. Robotics is also seen as the answer to China’s demographic problems, such as the ageing population and the shrinking workforce.
But the demand for robotics is being driven by government agencies and research institutions, rather than everyday consumers, for whom the products are still too expensive and not yet practical for home use. Humanoid robotics and robotic dogs have been popular in the entertainment industry but are yet to be useful in home settings.
Shares in Unitree, China’s leading robot-maker, have halved since they started trading in August.
“It doesn’t look like embodied intelligence could turn into profits in the in the mass market,” said Wang. Thin profit margins, rising rates in the US, and weak domestic demand were all contributing to a “general anxiety” among technology companies, she said.
China’s government wants local investors to invest their money domestically. China has in recent months restricted overseas investment, with more regulations taking effect from 1 December, but these moves have not led to greater investment in the Chinese markets.
Wang added that there was still optimism in other technology sectors, such as AI research and satellites, the latter because their links to the military indicates long term state support for the sector. And globally the AI boom is expected to last for at least another year.
On Monday, US AI company Anthropic, which makes the chatbot Claude, filed paperwork ahead of a planned IPO that could be the biggest stock market debuts of all time. The company is expected to bring in as much as $100bn.
China has no such blockbuster IPOs on the horizon. And despite pressure on policymakers to introduce stimulus measures to boost investment, none are expected to be announced during a politically sensitive period in China.
This week the top officials in the Chinese Communist party are gathering for the fifth plenum, an important meeting that will lay the groundwork for next year’s 21st Party Congress. The Congress is expected to anoint Xi Jinping, China’s leader, for a fourth term. There is no appetite for risky or potentially destabilising policy measures before then, even if there is a chance they could boost the economy.
Any stimulus measure would be “high risk”, Wang said. “What if it doesn’t work out? Then whoever came up with that policy, that guy would be held accountable”.

Technology description follows:
Compositions and Methods for Detecting Lymphatic Filariasis
Description of Technology
Lymphatic filariasis (elephantiasis; LF) is a neglected tropical disease characterized by painful deformation of the host. LF affects over 120 million people throughout the tropics and subtropics of Asia, Africa, the Western Pacific, and parts of the Caribbean and South America. LF results from infection with the filarial parasites
Wuchereria bancrofti
or
Brugia malayi.
Current methods of confirming active
( printed page 67594)
infection by
W. bancrofti
or
B. malayi
include microscopy and immunoassays using serum/plasma extracted from the patient. However, the sensitivity of microscopy detection varies among patients, and existing immunoassays show cross-reactivity with antibodies directed towards other parasites, such as
Onchocerca volvulus
or
Loa loa,
whose geographic distribution can overlap with the LF-causing filarial parasites.
This new technology addresses the limitation of cross-reactivity, presenting an opportunity for a directed assay towards the detection of
W. bancrofti
or
B. malayi.
Preliminary data against sera from LF-affected individuals indicates Wb4 is effective at detecting
B. malayi.
Wb4B, a modified version of recombinant Wb4 that lacks the nineteen (19) amino acid signal sequence of full-length Wb4, appears capable of isolation and purification by traditional molecular biology techniques and shows improved response in immunoassays.

and

prevalence.

Differentiation from other parasites with similar geographic footprints.

Abstract:
Established within the NSF by the America COMPETES Reauthorization Act of 2010 section 505, codified in the NSF Act of 1950, as amended, the National Center for Science and Engineering Statistics (NCSES) serves as a central Federal clearinghouse for the collection, interpretation, analysis, and dissemination of objective data on science, engineering, technology, and research and development for use by practitioners, researchers, policymakers, and the public.
The Survey of Earned Doctorates (SED) is part of NCSES' portfolio and collects data on individuals to provide information on science and engineering education and careers in the United States. The SED has been conducted annually since 1958 and is jointly sponsored by four Federal agencies (NSF/NCSES, National Institutes of Health, U.S. Department of Education/National Center for Education Statistics, and National Endowment for the Humanities) to avoid duplication of effort in collecting such data. It is an accurate, timely source of information on our Nation's highly educated individuals. This request to renew the information collection for three years is to cover the 2028 and 2029 SED survey cycles.
Data are obtained via Web survey from each person earning a research doctorate from an accredited U.S. institution at the time they receive the degree. Data are collected on their field of specialty, educational background, sources of support in graduate school, debt level, postgraduation plans, and demographic characteristics. NCSES publishes statistics from the survey in several reports. The survey will be collected in conformance with the Privacy Act of 1974. Responses from individuals are voluntary. NCSES will ensure that all individually identifiable information collected will be kept strictly confidential and will be used only for research or statistical purposes.
Use of the Information:
The Federal Government, policy makers, universities, researchers, and others use the information extensively. Results from the SED are used to assess characteristics of the doctorate population and trends in doctoral education and degrees. Data from the survey are published annually on the NCSES website in a publication series reporting on all fields of study, titled
Doctorate Recipients from U.S. Universities
(
https://ncses.nsf.gov/pubs/nsf26315). Information from the SED is also included in other series available online such as
Science and Engineering Indicators (https://ncses.nsf.gov/indicators).
In addition, access to tabular data from selected variables is available through the NCSES online data tool (
https://ncsesdata.nsf.gov/builder/sed) and the SED Restricted Data Analysis System (
https://ncsesdata.nsf.gov/rdas/#/).
Expected Respondents:
The SED is a census of all individuals receiving a research doctorate from an accredited U.S. academic institution in the academic year beginning July 1 and ending June 30 of the subsequent year. As such, the population for the 2028 SED consists of all individuals receiving a research doctorate in the 12-month period beginning July 1, 2027 and ending June 30, 2028. Likewise, the population for the 2029 SED consists of all individuals receiving a research doctorate in the 12-month period beginning July 1, 2028 and ending June 30, 2029. A research doctorate is a doctoral degree that (1) requires completion of an original intellectual contribution in the form of a dissertation or an equivalent culminating project (
e.g.,
musical composition) and (2) is not primarily intended as a degree for the practice of a profession. The most common research doctorate degree is the Ph.D. Recipients of professional doctoral degrees, such as MD, DDS, JD, DPharm, and PsyD, are not included in the SED. The 2028 and 2029 SED are expected to include about 615 separately reporting schools with eligible research doctoral programs from about 480 doctorate-granting institutions. Based on the historical trend, NCSES expects a stable turnout of research doctorates for the next few years with a nominal increase from the 2026 cycle estimating that approximately 62,000 individuals will receive a research doctorate from U.S. institutions in each of the 2028 cycle and the 2029 cycle.

articles.title: Determination That PEPCID RPD (Famotidine) Orally Disintegrating Tablets, 20 Milligrams and 40 Milligrams Were Not Withdrawn From Sale for Reasons of Safety or Effectiveness
articles.summary: The Food and Drug Administration (FDA, Agency, or we) has determined that PEPCID RPD (famotidine) orally disintegrating tablets, 20 milligrams (mg) and 40 mg, were not withdrawn from sale for reasons of safety or effectiveness. This determination will allow FDA to approve abbreviated new drug applications (ANDAs) for famotidine) orally disintegrating tablets, 20 mg and 40 mg, if all other legal and regulatory requirements are met.
articles.full_text:
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Section 505(j) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FD&C Act) (21 U.S.C. 355(j)) allows the submission of an ANDA to market a generic version of a previously approved drug product. To obtain approval, the ANDA applicant must show, among other things, that the generic drug product: (1) has the same active ingredient(s), dosage form, route of administration, strength, conditions of use, and (with certain exceptions) labeling as the listed drug, which is a version of the drug that was previously approved, and (2) is bioequivalent to the listed drug. ANDA applicants do not have to repeat the extensive clinical testing otherwise necessary to gain approval of a new drug application (NDA).
Section 505(j)(7) of the FD&C Act requires FDA to publish a list of all approved drugs. FDA publishes this list as part of the “Approved Drug Products With Therapeutic Equivalence Evaluations,” which is known generally as the “Orange Book.” Under FDA regulations, drugs are removed from the list if the Agency withdraws or suspends approval of the drug's NDA or ANDA for reasons of safety or effectiveness or if FDA determines that the listed drug was withdrawn from sale for reasons of safety or effectiveness (21 CFR 314.162).
A person may petition the Agency to determine, or the Agency may determine on its own initiative, whether a listed drug was withdrawn from sale for reasons of safety or effectiveness. This determination may be made at any time after the drug has been withdrawn from sale, but must be made prior to approving an ANDA that refers to the listed drug (§ 314.161 (21 CFR 314.161)). FDA may not approve an ANDA that does not refer to a listed drug.
                    PEPCID RPD (famotidine) orally disintegrating tablets, 20 mg and 40 mg, are the subject of NDA 020752, held by Merck & Co., Inc., and initially approved on May 29, 1998. PEPCID RPD is indicated for short term treatment of active duodenal ulcer, maintenance therapy for duodenal ulcer patients at reduced dosage after healing of an active ulcer, short term treatment of active benign gastric ulcer, short term treatment of gastroesophageal reflux disease, and treatment of pathological hypersecretory conditions (
                    e.g.,
                     Zollinger-Ellison Syndrome, multiple endocrine adenomas).
                
                    In a letter dated September 11, 2013, Merck Sharp & Dohme Corp., (Merck) notified FDA that PEPCID RPD (famotidine) orally disintegrating tablets, 20 mg and 40 mg, were being discontinued, and FDA moved the drug product to the “Discontinued Drug Product List” section of the Orange Book. In the same letter, Merck Sharp requested withdrawal of NDA 020752 for PEPCID RPD (famotidine) orally disintegrating tablets, 20 mg and 40 mg. In the 
                    Federal Register
                     of June 21, 2017 (82 FR 28322), FDA announced that it was withdrawing approval of NDA 020752, effective July 21, 2017.
                
Lachman Consultant Services, Inc. submitted a citizen petition dated June 29, 2026 (Docket No. FDA-2026-P-7178), under 21 CFR 10.30, requesting that the Agency determine whether PEPCID RPD (famotidine) orally disintegrating tablets, 20 mg and 40 mg, were withdrawn from sale for reasons of safety or effectiveness.
After considering the citizen petition and reviewing Agency records and based on the information we have at this time, FDA has determined under § 314.161 that PEPCID RPD (famotidine) orally disintegrating tablets, 20 mg and 40 mg, were not withdrawn for reasons of safety or effectiveness. The petitioner has identified no data or other information suggesting that these drug products were withdrawn for reasons of safety or effectiveness. We have carefully reviewed our files for records concerning the withdrawal of PEPCID RPD (famotidine) orally disintegrating tablets, 20 mg and 40 mg, from sale. We have also independently evaluated relevant literature and data for possible postmarketing adverse events. We have reviewed the available evidence and determined that this drug product was not withdrawn from sale for reasons of safety or effectiveness.
Accordingly, the Agency will continue to list PEPCID RPD (famotidine) orally disintegrating tablets, 20 mg and 40 mg, in the “Discontinued Drug Product List” section of the Orange Book. articles.full_text: The International Trade Administration (ITA) announces the launch of the U.S. Resources Management Industry Listing (RMIL), or "industry listing." The RMIL is intended to identify U.S. companies operating in water and wastewater treatment; waste management and recycling, including critical minerals recycling; air quality measuring, monitoring and control; monitoring and instrumentation; weather and forecasting; and other resources management sectors for informational, engagement, and policy support purposes. The RMIL will provide a platform for U.S. companies to market their products and services, raising their visibility with international buyers seeking to purchase U.S. resources management solutions. The RMIL supports ITA's efforts to promote American technologies and services to overseas partners and position U.S. companies to compete for international project opportunities. Eligible companies may now apply to be listed in the RMIL. The industry listing will be published online and will be maintained by the International Trade Administration's Office of Energy and Environmental Industries.

AGENCY:

ACTION:
Notice.
SUMMARY:
Section 106 of the Department of Housing and Urban Development Reform Act of 1989 (the HUD Reform Act) requires HUD to publish quarterly
Federal Register
notices of all regulatory waivers that HUD has approved. Each notice covers the quarterly period since the previous
Federal Register
notice. The purpose of this notice is to comply with the requirements of section 106 of the HUD Reform Act. This notice contains a list of regulatory waivers granted by HUD during the period beginning on January 1, 2026 and ending on March 31, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
For general information about this notice, contact Amanda Wahlig, Acting Associate General Counsel for Legislation and Regulations, Department of Housing and Urban Development, 451 7th Street SW, Room 10282, Washington, DC 20410-0500, telephone 202-708-3055 (this is not a toll-free number). HUD welcomes and is prepared to receive calls from individuals who are deaf or hard of hearing, as well as individuals with speech or communication disabilities. To learn more about how to make an accessible telephone call, please visit:
https://www.fcc.gov/consumers/guides/telecommunications-relay-service-trs.
For information concerning a particular waiver that was granted and for which public notice is provided in this document, contact the person whose name and address follow the description of the waiver granted in the accompanying list of waivers that have been granted in the first quarter of calendar year 2026.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Section 106 of the HUD Reform Act added a new section 7(q) to the Department of Housing and Urban Development Act (42 U.S.C. 3535(q)), which provides that:
1. Any waiver of a regulation must be in writing and must specify the grounds for approving the waiver;
2. Authority to approve a waiver of a regulation may be delegated by the Secretary only to an individual of Assistant Secretary or equivalent rank, and the person to whom authority to waive is delegated must also have authority to issue the particular regulation to be waived;
3. Not less than quarterly, the Secretary must notify the public of all waivers of regulations that HUD has approved, by publishing a notice in the
Federal Register
. These notices (each covering the period since the most recent previous notification) shall:
a. Identify the project, activity, or undertaking involved;
b. Describe the nature of the provision waived and the designation of the provision;
c. Indicate the name and title of the person who granted the waiver request;
d. Describe briefly the grounds for approval of the request; and
e. State how additional information about a particular waiver may be obtained.
Section 106 of the HUD Reform Act also contains requirements applicable to waivers of HUD handbook provisions that are not relevant to the purpose of this notice.
This notice follows procedures provided in HUD's Statement of Policy on Waiver of Regulations and Directives issued on April 22, 1991 (56 FR 16337). In accordance with those procedures and with the requirements of section 106 of the HUD Reform Act, waivers of regulations are granted by the Assistant Secretary with jurisdiction over the regulations for which a waiver was requested. In those cases in which a General Deputy Assistant Secretary granted the waiver, the General Deputy Assistant Secretary was serving in the absence of the Assistant Secretary in accordance with the office's Order of Succession.
This notice covers waivers of regulations granted by HUD from January 1, 2026 through March 31, 2026. For ease of reference, the waivers granted by HUD are listed by HUD program office (for example, the Office of Community Planning and Development, the Office of Fair Housing and Equal Opportunity, the Office of Housing, and the Office of Public and Indian Housing, etc.). Within each program office grouping, the waivers are listed sequentially by the regulatory section of title 24 of the Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) that is being waived. For example, a waiver of a provision in 24 CFR part 58 would be listed before a waiver of a provision in 24 CFR part 570.
Where more than one regulatory provision is involved in the grant of a particular waiver request, the action is listed under the section number of the first regulatory requirement that appears in 24 CFR and that is being waived. For example, a waiver of both § 58.73 and § 58.74 would appear sequentially in the listing under § 58.73.
Waiver of regulations that involve the same initial regulatory citation are in time sequence beginning with the earliest-dated regulatory waiver.
Should HUD receive additional information about waivers granted during the period covered by this report (the first quarter of calendar year 2026) before the next report is published (the second quarter of calendar year 2026), HUD will include any additional waivers granted for the first quarter in the next report.
( printed page 67599)
Accordingly, information about approved waiver requests pertaining to HUD regulations is provided in the Appendix that follows this notice.

SUMMARY:
Notice is hereby given that on October 20, 2026, the presiding administrative law judge (“ALJ”) issued an Initial Determination on Violation of Section 337 and Recommended Determination on Remedy and Bond. The Commission is soliciting submissions on public interest issues raised by the recommended relief should the Commission find a violation. This notice is soliciting comments from the public and interested government agencies only.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Joelle Justus, Esq., Office of the General Counsel, U.S. International Trade Commission, 500 E Street SW, Washington, DC 20436, telephone (202) 205-2593. Copies of non-confidential documents filed in connection with this investigation may be viewed on the Commission's electronic docket (EDIS) at

EDIS3Help@usitc.gov.

https://www.usitc.gov.
Hearing-impaired persons are advised that information on this matter can be obtained by contacting the Commission's TDD terminal on (202) 205-1810.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Section 337 of the Tariff Act of 1930 provides that, if the Commission finds a violation, it shall exclude the articles concerned from the United States unless, after considering the effect of such exclusion upon the public health and welfare, competitive conditions in the United States economy, the production of like or directly competitive articles in the United States, and United States consumers, it finds that such articles should not be excluded from entry. (19 U.S.C. 1337(d)(1)). A similar provision applies to cease and desist orders. (19 U.S.C. 1337(f)(1)).
The Commission is soliciting submissions on public interest issues raised by the recommended relief should the Commission find a violation. The recommended relief includes a limited exclusion order directed to vaporizer devices, cartridges used therewith, and components thereof imported, sold for importation, and/or sold after importation by respondents Glas, Inc. and Glas, LLC that infringe claims 1, 5, 7, 15-16, and 18-21 of U.S. Patent No. 11,134,722 and claims 1, 5, and 8 of U.S. Patent No. 11,606,981. The recommended relief also includes a cease and desist order directed to the Glas respondents. Parties are to file public interest submissions pursuant to 19 CFR 210.50(a)(4).
The Commission is interested in further development of the record on the public interest in this investigation. Accordingly, members of the public and interested government agencies are invited to file submissions of no more than five (5) pages, inclusive of attachments, concerning the public interest in light of the ALJ's Recommended Determination on Remedy and Bonding issued in this investigation on October 20, 2026. Comments should address whether issuance of the recommended remedial orders in this investigation, should the Commission find a violation, would affect the public health and welfare in the United States, competitive conditions in the United States economy, the production of like or directly competitive articles in the United States, or United States consumers.
In particular, the Commission is interested in comments that:
(i) Explain how the articles potentially subject to the recommended remedial orders are used in the United States;
(ii) Identify any public health, safety, or welfare concerns in the United States relating to the recommended orders;
(iii) Identify like or directly competitive articles that complainant, its licensees, or third parties make in the United States which could replace the subject articles if they were to be excluded;
(iv) Indicate whether complainant, complainant's licensees, and/or third-party suppliers have the capacity to replace the volume of articles potentially subject to the recommended orders within a commercially reasonable time; and
(v) Explain how the recommended orders would impact consumers in the United States.
Written submissions must be filed no later than by close of business on November 19, 2026.
Persons filing written submissions must file the original document electronically on or before the deadlines stated above pursuant to 19 CFR 210.4(f). Submissions should refer to the investigation number (“Inv. No. 337-TA-1464”) in a prominent place on the cover page and/or the first page. (

articles.summary: The United States (U.S.) Department of Energy (DOE) is issuing this notice to advise the public that DOE added helium to the DOE Critical Material List. This notice also provides the link to the assessment that forms the justification for including helium on the Critical Material List. Helium is non-substitutable for multiple critical energy functions, including: semiconductor manufacturing, leak testing natural gas infrastructure, and quantum computing, along with being essential to key medical...
articles.full_text:
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
                    Section 7002(a)(2) of the Energy Act of 2020 (Pub. L. 116-260, div. Z, 134 Stat. 2418) defines “critical materials” to be: any non-fuel mineral, element, substance, or material that the Secretary of Energy determines has high risk for supply chain disruption and serves an essential function in one or more energy technologies, including technologies that produce, transmit, store, and conserve energy (referred to here as a critical material for energy) or a critical mineral (as designated by the Secretary of the Interior).[] 
                    
                
                    On August 4, 2023, DOE published its Notice of Final Determination on 2023 DOE Critical Materials List (“Critical Materials List”).[] 
                    
                     The Critical Materials List includes the following:
                
                    Critical materials for energy:
                     aluminum, cobalt, copper*, dysprosium, electrical steel* (grain-oriented electrical steel, non-grain-oriented electrical steel, and amorphous steel), fluorine, gallium, iridium, lithium, magnesium, natural graphite, neodymium, nickel, platinum, praseodymium, terbium, silicon*, and silicon carbide*.[] 
                    
                
                    Critical minerals:
                     The Secretary of the Interior, acting through the Director of the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS), published a 2022 final list of critical minerals that includes the following 50 minerals: Aluminum, antimony, arsenic, barite, beryllium, bismuth, cerium, cesium, chromium, cobalt, dysprosium, erbium, europium, fluorspar, gadolinium, gallium, germanium, graphite, hafnium, holmium, indium, iridium, lanthanum, lithium, lutetium, magnesium, manganese, neodymium, nickel, niobium, palladium, platinum, praseodymium, rhodium, rubidium, ruthenium, samarium, scandium, tantalum, tellurium, terbium, thulium, tin, titanium, tungsten, vanadium, ytterbium, yttrium, zinc, and zirconium.
                
                    The critical materials for energy included on the Critical Material List are based on the criticality assessed in the short- and medium-term. A detailed description of DOE's methodology can be found in its Critical Minerals Assessment published on its website in July 2023.[] 
                    
                     On May 22, 2025, metallurgical grade coal for steelmaking was added to DOE's list of critical materials for energy.[] 
                    
                
                    By this notice, the Secretary of Energy advises the public of the addition of helium to DOE's Critical Material List. The assessment that forms the justification for including helium on the Critical Material List can be found on DOE's website: 
                    https://www.energy.gov/cmm/what-are-critical-materials-and-critical-minerals.
                     The assessment concludes that helium is needed globally for semiconductor manufacturing and other key energy applications. Meeting the policy goal of building U.S. SI infrastructure will require expansion of semiconductor production and thereby supports the determination that helium is a DOE critical material.
                
                    Furthermore, this action directly supports the President's policy goal of “Winning the AI Race: America's AI Action Plan” [] 
                    
                     and “Advancing United States Leadership in Artificial Intelligence Infrastructure”.[] 
                    
                
Signing Authority
                    This document of the Department of Energy was signed on October 21, 2026, by Audrey Robertson, Assistant Secretary, Office of Critical Minerals and Energy Innovation, pursuant to delegated authority from the Secretary of Energy. That document with the original signature and date is maintained by DOE. For administrative purposes only, and in compliance with requirements of the Office of the Federal Register, the undersigned DOE Federal Register Liaison Officer has been authorized to sign and submit the document in electronic format for publication, as an official document of the Department of Energy. This administrative process in no way alters the legal effect of this document upon publication in the 
                    Federal Register
                    .
                
                    Signed in Washington, DC, on October 23, 2026.
Jennifer Hartzell,
Alternate Federal Register Liaison Officer, U.S. Department of Energy.

AGENCY:
U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission.
ACTION:
Call for nominations.
SUMMARY:
The U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) is soliciting nominations for the position of an Interventional Radiologist on the Advisory Committee on the Medical Uses of Isotopes (ACMUI). Nominees should currently be practicing as an Interventional Radiologist.
DATES:
Nominations are due on or before December 28, 2026.
Nomination Process:
Submit an electronic copy of resume or curriculum vitae, along with a cover letter, to Ms. Sarah Hoenig,
Sarah.Hoenig@nrc.gov.
The cover letter should describe the nominee's current duties and responsibilities and express the nominee's interest in the position. Please ensure that the resume or curriculum vitae includes the following information, if applicable: education; certification(s); professional association and committee membership activities; duties and responsibilities in current and previous clinical, research, and/or academic position(s).
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Sarah Hoenig, U.S Nuclear Regulatory Commission, Office of Nuclear Material Safety and Safeguards; 301-415-3284;
Sarah.Hoenig@nrc.gov.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
ACMUI members possess the medical and technical skills needed to address evolving issues. The current membership is comprised of the following professionals: (a) nuclear medicine physician; (b) nuclear cardiologist; (c) two radiation oncologists; (d) diagnostic radiologist; (e) therapy medical physicist; (f) nuclear medicine physicist; (g) nuclear pharmacist; (h) radiation safety officer; (i) patients' rights advocate; (j) Food and Drug Administration representative; (k) Agreement State representative; and (l) interventional radiologist (vacant). For additional information about membership on the ACMUI, visit the ACMUI Membership web page,
http://www.nrc.gov/about-nrc/regulatory/advisory/acmui/membership.html.
The ACMUI Interventional Radiologist provides advice on issues associated with the regulation of interventional radiology applications of byproduct material. This advice includes providing input on NRC proposed rules and guidance, providing recommendations on the training and experience requirements for Authorized Interventional Radiologists, identifying medical events associated with these uses, evaluating non-routine uses of byproduct material, bringing key issues in the interventional radiology community to the attention of NRC staff, radiation safety and NRC medical-use policy. This individual is appointed based on his or her educational background, certification(s), work experience, involvement and/or leadership in professional society activities, and other information obtained in letters or during the selection process.
Nominees must be U.S. citizens and be able to devote approximately 160 hours per year to ACMUI business. Members are expected to attend semi-annual full-day virtual meetings and to participate in other shorter teleconferences or virtual meetings, as needed. ACMUI members who present during the annual ACMUI Commission Briefing Meeting, may need to travel to attend these meetings in-person at NRC HQs in Rockville, MD. Committee members currently serve a four-year term and may be considered for reappointment to an additional term.
( printed page 67624)
Members who are not Federal employees at the time of their appointment are compensated for their service. In addition, members are reimbursed for travel (including per diem in lieu of subsistence) and are reimbursed secretarial and correspondence expenses. Full-time Federal employees are reimbursed for travel expenses only.
Security Background Check:
The selected nominee will undergo a thorough security background check. Security paperwork may take the nominee several weeks to complete.
Nominees will also be required to complete a financial disclosure statement to avoid conflicts of interest.
Dated at Rockville, Maryland, this 23 of October, 2026.

Abstract:
The STOP Violence Against Women Formula Grant Program was authorized through the Violence Against Women Act of 1994 (VAWA), amended and reauthorized in 2000, 2005, 2013 and 2022. The STOP (Services, Training, Officers, and Prosecutors) Violence Against Women Formula Grant Program provides funding to states and territories for use by state, local, and Indian Tribal governments, courts, and victim service providers. This program enhances the capacity of local communities to develop and strengthen effective law enforcement and prosecution strategies to combat domestic violence, dating violence, sexual assault and stalking and to develop and strengthen comprehensive, holistic victim services. The grant funds must be distributed by STOP state administrators to subgrantees according to a statutory formula.
Each state and territory must allocate 25 percent for law enforcement, 25 percent for prosecutors, 30 percent for victim services (of which at least 10 percent must be distributed to culturally specific community-based organizations), 5 percent to state and local courts, and 15 percent for discretionary distribution. VAWA provides for a 25 percent match requirement imposed on grant funds under the STOP Violence Against Women Formula Grant Program. Thus, a grant made under this program may not cover more than 75 percent of the total costs of the project being funded. The state is exempted from matching the portion of the state award that goes to a victim service provider for victim services or that goes to a tribe. Territories are also exempted in full. States can apply to have the match requirement waived by submitting a petition to OVW and a demonstrating financial need. At the time of closeout, OVW will look at the entities and purposes of funds and determine the required match amount.
The purpose of this information collection is to provide a worksheet for documenting the amount of matching funds required at the closeout of a specific fiscal year award under the STOP Violence Against Women Formula Grant Program. articles.full_text: This notice announces the decision of the Secretary of Homeland Security (Secretary) to suspend the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands (CNMI) Economic Vitality & Security Travel Authorization Program (EVS-TAP). EVS-TAP allows prescreened nationals of the People's Republic of China (PRC) to travel to the CNMI without a visa for temporary visits under specified conditions. Pursuant to the Immigration and Nationality Act and Department of Homeland Security (DHS) regulations, the Secretary has broad authority to suspend the program for good cause, including threats to national security, law enforcement interests, and immigration enforcement. The Secretary has determined that there is good cause to suspend EVS-TAP, while DHS, in consultation with the Secretary of State and the Secretary of the Interior, evaluates the program.

articles.full_text:
Commission staff coordinated with the staff of the North American Electric Reliability Corporation (NERC) to conduct the annual oversight of NERC's Find, Fix, Track and Report (FFT) program, as outlined in the Commission's March 15, 2012 order,[] 
                    
                     and the Compliance Exception (CE) Program, as proposed by NERC's September 18, 2015 annual compliance filing and accepted by delegated order.[] 
                    
                
Commission staff reviewed a sample of 29 of 206 FFTs and 34 of 1,619 CEs submitted by NERC between October 2024 and September 2025.
Commission staff found that the FFT and CE programs are meeting the Commission's expectations in accordance with FFT Order, with limited exceptions. Specifically, Commission staff identified one instance of an FFT in which the original description was incomplete. Staff also noted in two instances of CEs that the originally posted description had an inaccurate noncompliance start or end date. All 63 FFTs and CEs have been adequately remediated, and the root cause of each noncompliance was clearly identified. Commission staff also reviewed the supporting information for these FFTs and CEs and agreed with the final risk determinations for all 63 noncompliances, which clearly identified the factors affecting the risk prior to mitigation (such as potential and actual risk) and actual harm. Further, no FFTs or CEs sampled contained any material misrepresentations by the registered entities. Commission staff found that the Regional Entities appropriately identified all 63 of the sampled noncompliances as appropriate to be processed as FFTs and CEs.
                    Dated: October 22, 2026.
Debbie-Anne A. Reese,
Secretary.

The staff of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC or Commission) will prepare an environmental document that will discuss the environmental impacts of the Phase IX Project (Project) involving construction and operation of facilities by Florida Gas Transmission Company, LLC (FGT) in Mississippi, Alabama, and Florida. The Commission will use this environmental document in its decision-making process to determine whether the project is in the public convenience and necessity.
This notice announces the opening of the scoping process the Commission will use to gather input from the public and interested agencies regarding the project. As part of the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) review process, the Commission takes into account concerns the public may have about proposals and the environmental impacts that could result from its action whenever it considers the issuance of a Certificate of Public Convenience and Necessity. This gathering of public input is referred to as “scoping.” The main goal of the scoping process is to focus the analysis in the environmental document on the important environmental issues. Additional information about the Commission's NEPA process is described below in the
NEPA Process and Environmental Document
section of this notice.
By this notice, the Commission requests public comments on the scope of issues to address in the environmental document. To ensure that your comments are timely and properly recorded, please submit your comments so that the Commission receives them in Washington, DC on or before 5:00 p.m. Eastern Time on November 23, 2026. Comments may be submitted in written form. Further details on how to submit comments are provided in the
Public Participation
section of this notice.
Your comments should focus on the potential environmental effects, reasonable alternatives, and measures to avoid or lessen environmental impacts. Your input will help the Commission staff determine what issues they need to evaluate in the environmental document. Commission staff will consider all written comments during the preparation of the environmental document.
If you submitted comments on this project to the Commission
before
the opening of this docket on September 9, 2026, you will need to file those comments in Docket No. CP26-578-000 to ensure they are considered as part of this proceeding.
This notice is being sent to the Commission's current environmental mailing list for this project. State and local government representatives should notify their constituents of this proposed project and encourage them to comment on their areas of concern.
If you are a landowner receiving this notice, a pipeline company representative may contact you about the acquisition of an easement to construct, operate, and maintain the proposed facilities. The company would seek to negotiate a mutually acceptable easement agreement. You are not required to enter into an agreement. However, if the Commission approves the project, the Natural Gas Act conveys the right of eminent domain to the company. Therefore, if you and the company do not reach an easement agreement, the pipeline company could initiate condemnation proceedings in court. In such instances, compensation would be determined by a judge in accordance with state law. The Commission does not subsequently grant, exercise, or oversee the exercise of that eminent domain authority. The courts have exclusive authority to
( printed page 67561)
handle eminent domain cases; the Commission has no jurisdiction over these matters.
FGT provided landowners with a fact sheet prepared by the FERC entitled “An Interstate Natural Gas Facility On My Land? What Do I Need To Know?” which addresses typically asked questions, including the use of eminent domain and how to participate in the Commission's proceedings. This fact sheet along with other landowner topics of interest are available for viewing on the FERC website (

www.ferc.gov) under the link to FERC Online. Using eComment is an easy method for submitting brief, text-only comments on a project;

www.ferc.gov) under the link to FERC Online. With eFiling, you can provide comments in a variety of formats by attaching them as a file with your submission. New eFiling users must first create an account by clicking on “eRegister.” You will be asked to select the type of filing you are making; a comment on a particular project is considered a “Comment on a Filing”; or
(3) You can file a paper copy of your comments by mailing them to the Commission. Be sure to reference the project docket number (CP26-578-000) on your letter. Submissions sent via the U.S. Postal Service must be addressed to: Debbie-Anne A. Reese, Secretary, Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, 888 First Street NE, Room 1A, Washington, DC 20426. Submissions sent via any other carrier must be addressed to: Debbie-Anne A. Reese, Secretary, Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, 12225 Wilkins Avenue, Rockville, MD 20852.

to register for eSubscription.

The U.S. Coast Guard announces that it is adding the Federal Republic of Somalia to the Port Security Advisory.
DATES:

FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
For information about this document call or email Mr. Edward Munoz, Division Chief, International Port Security Assessments, U.S. Coast Guard, telephone 202-372-2122,
HQS-DG-IPSProgramHQs@uscg.mil.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background and Purpose
The authority for this notice is 5 U.S.C. 552(a) (“Administrative Procedure Act”), 46 U.S.C. 70110 (“Maritime Transportation Security Act”), and Department of Homeland Security Delegation No. 0170.1(II)(97)(f). As delegated, section 70110(a) authorizes the U.S. Coast Guard to impose conditions of entry on vessels arriving in U.S. waters from ports that the U.S. Coast Guard has not found to maintain effective antiterrorism measures. Accordingly, the U.S. Coast Guard has determined that Somalia is not maintaining effective antiterrorism measures in its ports and is imposing conditions of entry on vessels arriving to the U.S. from the ports of Somalia.
With this notice, the current list of countries assessed and not maintaining effective antiterrorism measures is as follows: Cambodia, Cameroon, Comoros, Cuba, Democratic People's Republic of Korea (North Korea), Equatorial Guinea, Gambia (The), Guinea-Bissau, Haiti, Iran, Iraq, Libya, Madagascar, Micronesia (Federated States of), Nauru, Sao Tome and Principe, Seychelles, Somalia, Sudan, Suriname, Syria, Timor-Leste, Venezuela, and Yemen. The current Port Security Advisory is available at:
http://www.dco.uscg.mil/Our-Organization/Assistant-Commandant-for-Prevention-Policy-CG-5P/International-Domestic-Port-Assessment/.

Abstract:
The Organ Procurement and Transplantation Network (OPTN) is a public-private partnership that links professionals involved in the U.S. donation, procurement, and transplantation system. The OPTN focuses on promoting long, healthy, and productive lives for people with organ failure. AGENCY:
U.S. Customs and Border Protection, Department of Homeland Security.
                    SUMMARY:
This document provides notice to customs brokers that the annual user fee that is assessed for each permit held by a customs broker, whether an individual, partnership, association, or corporation, is due no later than January 29, 2027. Pursuant to fee adjustments required by the Fixing America's Surface Transportation Act (FAST Act) and the U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) regulations, the customs broker permit user fee payable for calendar year 2027 will be $190.88.
                    DATES:
Payment of the 2027 Customs Broker Permit User Fee is due no later than January 29, 2027.
            
                SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background
                    Pursuant to section 111.96 of title 19 of the Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) (19 CFR 111.96(c)), U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) assesses an annual user fee for each customs broker permit granted to an individual, partnership, association, or corporation. The CBP regulations provide that this fee is payable each calendar year for a national permit held by a customs broker and must be paid by the due date published annually in the 
                    Federal Register
                    . See19 CFR 24.22(h) and (i); 19 CFR 111.96(c).
                
Section 24.22 of title 19 of the CFR (19 CFR 24.22) sets forth the terms and conditions for when fees for certain services, including specific customs user fees, are required. The specific customs user fee amounts that appear in 19 CFR 24.22 are not the actual fees but represent the base year amounts that are subject to adjustment each fiscal year in accordance with the Fixing America's Surface Transportation Act (FAST Act) (Pub. L. 114-94, December 4, 2015). Section 32201 of the FAST Act amended section 13031 of the Consolidated Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act (COBRA) of 1985 (19 U.S.C. 58c) by requiring the Secretary of the Treasury to adjust certain customs COBRA user fees and corresponding limitations to reflect certain increases in inflation. Paragraph (k) of section 24.22 of title 19 of the CFR (19 CFR 24.22(k)) sets forth the methodology to adjust fees for inflation and to determine the change in inflation, including the factor by which the fees and limitations will be adjusted, if necessary.
                    Customs brokers are subject to an annual customs broker permit user fee calculated using the base year amount in Appendix A to 19 CFR part 24, as adjusted by the terms in 19 CFR 24.22(k). 
                    See19 U.S.C. 58c(a)(7) and 19 CFR 24.22(h). In accordance with 19 CFR 24.22, CBP determines annually whether an adjustment to the fees and limitations is necessary and publishes a 
                    Federal Register
                     notice specifying the amount of the fees and limitations for each fiscal year. On July 31, 2026, CBP published a 
                    Federal Register
                     notice, entitled Customs User Fees To Be Adjusted for Inflation in Fiscal Year 2027 (CBP Decision 26-14), which announced, among other fee adjustments, that the annual customs broker permit user fee will increase to $190.88 for calendar year 2027. 
                    See91 FR 48398.
                
                    Thus, as required by 19 CFR 24.22, CBP provided notice in the 
                    Federal Register
                     of the annual fee amount at least 60 days prior to the date that the payment is due for each customs broker national permit. This document notifies customs brokers that, for calendar year 2027, the due date for payment of the annual customs broker permit user fee is January 29, 2027. If a customs broker fails to pay the annual customs broker permit user fee by January 29, 2027, the national permit is revoked by operation of law. 
                    See19 CFR 111.45(b) and 111.96(c).
                
                    Customs brokers are strongly encouraged to submit the payment electronically via the eCBP portal located at 
                    https://e.cbp.dhs.gov/brokers/#/home.
                     Customs brokers who are first-time users of the eCBP portal must create a 
                    Login.gov
                     account. Instructions and training resources—such as user and quick reference guides for customs brokers on how to create a 
                    Login.gov
                     account and how to use the eCBP portal—can be found on CBP's website at 
                    https://www.cbp.gov/trade/eCBP.
                     CBP will also accept payments at the processing center as defined in 19 CFR 111.1, in accordance with the remittance procedures in 19 CFR 24.22(i).
                
                    Susan S. Thomas,
Executive Assistant Commissioner, Office of Trade.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Background
NEMSAC is authorized under Section 31108 of the Moving Ahead for Progress in the 21st Century Act of 2012, codified at 42 U.S.C. 300d-4 as a Federal Advisory Committee. The purpose of NEMSAC is to serve as a nationally recognized council of emergency medical services (EMS) representatives to provide advice to and consult with:
a. The Federal Interagency Committee on Emergency Medical Services (FICEMS) on matters relating to EMS issues; and
b. The Secretary of Transportation on matters relating to EMS issues affecting DOT.
NEMSAC provides an important national forum for the non-Federal deliberation of national EMS issues and serves as a platform for advice on DOT's national EMS activities. NEMSAC also provides advice and recommendations to the FICEMS.
II. Agenda
At the meeting, the agenda will cover the following topics:
NHTSA Initiatives
Updates from Federal Partners
FICEMS Strategic Plan for National Implementation of Prehospital Blood Transfusion
Request for Consultation and Advice
General Informational Sessions
Strategic Planning for NEMSAC
Public Comment Period
III. Background on FICEMS Strategic Plan for National Implementation of Prehospital Blood Transfusion
Severe bleeding is the leading cause of preventable death in trauma patients. Evidence demonstrates that prompt prehospital blood transfusion can save an estimated 37 percent of trauma patients experiencing severe bleeding, whereas every minute of delay increases mortality risk by 11 percent. The draft FICEMS Strategic Plan for National Implementation of Prehospital Blood Transfusion (2026-2028) aims to prevent 10,000 deaths annually and achieve a 5 percent reduction in overall trauma mortality from severe bleeding by 2028.
The Council will deliberate on a letter from the Designated Federal Officer requesting consultation and advice on the FICEMS Strategic Plan for National Implementation of Prehospital Blood Transfusion. The Council will also deliberate on the Request for Information (RFI) published in the
Federal Register
on October 5, 2026. The RFI solicits public comments on feasibility, operational challenges, data linkage, and logistics associated with meeting the following national targets (key performance indicators or KPIs) across three core pillars:
Goal 1: Integrated Informatics
Pediatric Pre-Arrival Instructions:
Increase the percentage of children with life-threatening bleeding post-crash receiving 911 pre-arrival instructions from a calendar year (CY) 2025 baseline of 20 percent to a 2028 target of 25 percent.
Overall Pre-Arrival Instructions:
Increase the percentage of all patients with life-threatening bleeding post-crash receiving 911 pre-arrival instructions from a CY 2025 baseline of 20 percent to a 2028 target of 25 percent.
Goal 2: Systems Innovation
Ground EMS Agency Programs:
Expand the total number of ground EMS
( printed page 67650)
agencies with operational prehospital blood transfusion programs from a CY 2026 baseline of 450 agencies to a 2028 target of 2,028 agencies.
Goal 3: Clinical Excellence
Pediatric Prehospital Transfusion:
Increase the percentage of pediatric patients with life-threatening bleeding post-crash receiving prehospital blood transfusion from a CY 2025 baseline of 7 percent to a 2028 target of 28 percent.
Overall Prehospital Transfusion:
Increase the percentage of all patients with life-threatening bleeding post-crash receiving prehospital blood transfusion from a CY 2025 baseline of 4 percent to a 2028 target of 16 percent.
IV. Public Participation
This meeting will be open to the public. We are committed to providing equal access to this meeting for all participants. People with disabilities who need accommodation should send a request to the individual in the
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT
section of this notice no later than October 26, 2026.
A period of time will be allotted for comments from members of the public attending the meeting. Members of the public may present questions and comments to the Council using the live chat feature available during the meeting. Members of the public may also submit materials, questions, and comments in advance to the individual listed in the
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT

I. Introduction
On June 30, 2026, Cboe Clear U.S., LLC (“CCUS”) filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission (“Commission”) an application on Form CA-1 under Section 17A of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (“Exchange Act”) [1]
seeking to register as a clearing agency to provide central counterparty (“CCP”) services for binary options that are securities.[2]
In its application, CCUS requests temporary registration as a clearing agency under Section 17A(b) of the Exchange Act and pursuant to 17 CFR 240.17ab2-1 (“Rule 17Ab2-1”).[3]
Notice of the application (“Notice”) was published for comment in the
Federal Register
on July 24, 2026.[4]
CCUS amended its application on July 7 and 17, August 18, September 4, and October 1,[5]
2026 (as amended, “Application”).[6]
The Commission received one comment letter, as well as a response from CCUS.[7]
The comment letter supports approval of CCUS's request for temporary registration as a “stopgap;” as to permanent registration, it raises concerns as to the risk of vertically integrated solutions and requests that the Commission consider the capital costs and risks of a more fragmented clearing structure.[8]
The comment letter received, and CCUS's response thereto,[9]
are discussed in Parts III and IV.
This order grants CCUS's request for temporary registration as a clearing agency with an exemption from certain requirements as to which the Commission is directed to make a determination under Sections 17A(b)(3)(B) and (F) for a period of 18 months from the date of this order, for the reasons set forth in Parts III and IV below.
II. Statutory Standard for Registration as a Clearing Agency
Clearing agencies are broadly defined under the Exchange Act and undertake a variety of functions,[10]
including providing the services of a CCP.[11]
Pursuant to Section 17A of the Exchange Act and Rule 17Ab2-1 thereunder, an entity that meets the definition of a clearing agency must register with the Commission.[12]
Section 17A(b)(1) also states that, upon the Commission's motion or upon a clearing agency's application, the Commission may conditionally or unconditionally exempt a clearing agency from any provisions of Section 17A or the rules or regulations thereunder if the Commission finds that such exemption is consistent with the public interest, the protection of investors, and the purposes of Section 17A, including the prompt and accurate clearance and settlement of securities transactions and the safeguarding of securities and funds.[13]
In addition to the requirements set forth in Rule 17Ab2-1, Section 19(a)(1) of the Exchange Act establishes the standard for Commission review of an application for registration as a clearing agency. Pursuant thereto, the Commission shall grant registration of a clearing agency if it finds that the requirements of the Exchange Act and the rules and regulations thereunder with respect to the applicant are satisfied.[14]
The Commission shall deny such registration if it does not make such finding.[15]
The requirements of the Exchange Act applicable to clearing agencies are set forth in Section 17A and the rules and regulations thereunder.[16]
Accordingly,
( printed page 67625)
to grant CCUS's Application for registration as a clearing agency, the Commission must find that the Application satisfies the requirements of Section 17A(b) of the Exchange Act and rules and regulations thereunder, including the determinations set forth in paragraphs (A) through (I) of Section 17A(b)(3) of the Exchange Act.[17]
Pursuant to Rule 17Ab2-1(c), the Commission, upon the request of a clearing agency, may grant registration of the clearing agency but exempt the registrant from one or more of the requirements as to which the Commission is directed to make a determination pursuant to Section 17A(b)(3) of the Exchange Act, provided that any such registration shall be effective only for eighteen months from the date the registration is made effective (or such longer period as the Commission may provide by order).[18]
After a clearing agency's application for registration is granted, the clearing agency must continue to satisfy the requirements of the Exchange Act and the rules and regulations thereunder. In the context of temporary registration, the clearing agency must satisfy the requirements of the Exchange Act and the rules and regulations thereunder, except as to requirements, rules, or regulations to which an exemption has been provided. The Commission has explained that “[a]n approval of clearing agency registration does not mean that no further modifications of the applicant's rules, systems, procedures, or practices are needed.” [19]
Rather, the Commission stated that a registered clearing agency's obligation to continue to satisfy the requirements of the Exchange Act and the rules and regulations thereunder means that “[t]he self-regulatory obligations of [a] fully registered clearing agenc[y] cannot end” after registration.[20]
To ensure such compliance, the Commission stated that it “will continue to use its oversight, inspection, and enforcement authority as necessary and appropriate to further the purposes of the [Exchange] Act.” [21]
III. Review of Application Under Statutory Standard for Registration
Consistent with the requirements in Sections 17A and 19(a)(1) of the Exchange Act described above, the Commission below analyzes the Application against each of the statutory requirements under Section 17A(b)(3)(A) through (I) to be registered as a clearing agency.[22]

The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) is announcing
( printed page 67566)
the availability of the latest major release of the MOtor Vehicle Emission Simulator (MOVES) model, MOVES6. MOVES6 is the latest version of the EPA's state-of-the-science modeling tool for estimating emissions from cars, trucks, buses, and motorcycles based on the latest data and regulations. MOVES6 is available for use in State Implementation Plans (SIPs) and transportation conformity analyses. This notice starts a two-year grace period before MOVES6 will be required for use in transportation conformity determinations, both in new regional emissions analyses and in new hot-spot analyses.
DATES:

This announcement starts a two-year transportation conformity grace period that ends on October 27, 2028. After this date, MOVES6 will be required for use as the latest EPA emissions model for new transportation conformity analyses other than California in both regional emissions analyses and in hot-spot analyses.

AGENCY:
Federal Bureau of Investigation, Department of Justice.
ACTION:
Final rule.
SUMMARY:
The United States Department of Justice (“Department”) is amending several of its regulations pertaining to the National Instant Criminal Background Check System (“NICS” or “system”) of the Federal Bureau of Investigation (“FBI”) to authorize Federal Firearm Licensees (“FFLs” or “licensees”) to use NICS for purposes of voluntarily conducting employment background checks relating to certain current or prospective FFL employees. This final rule describes in more detail how, upon its effective date, FFLs will be able to conduct “firearm handler background checks” (“FHCs”) of “eligible employees.”
DATES:
This final rule is effective November 27, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Jill A. Montgomery, Assistant Section Chief, Federal Bureau of Investigation, Criminal Justice Information Services Division, NICS Section; Telephone: (304) 625-0606 (this is not a toll-free number).

I. Executive Summary
A. Summary of the Regulatory Action
As part of combatting firearms trafficking and straw purchasing and advancing other goals, Congress passed the Bipartisan Safer Communities Act (“BSCA”), requiring the Attorney General, in relevant part, to promulgate regulations authorizing licensees to voluntarily use NICS as part of the licensees' employment background checks of current or prospective FFL employees.
SeePublic Law 117-159, sec. 12004, 136 Stat. 1313, 1326-1332 (2022); 34 U.S.C. 40901(b)(2). On December 12, 2024, the Department published a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (“NPRM”) in the
Federal Register
seeking comments on the Department's proposed revisions to 28 CFR part 25 that, if finalized, would allow FFLs to voluntarily conduct FHCs of eligible FFL employees.
See
Bipartisan Safer Communities Act of 2022—Criteria for National Instant Criminal Background Check System (“NICS”) Background Checks of Firearm Handlers, 89 FR 100424 (Dec. 12, 2024). With limited exceptions discussed in Section V of this rule, the amendments to 28 CFR part 25 will be finalized as proposed in the NPRM.
B. Summary of Costs and Benefits
As proposed in the NPRM, this rule will impose little to no costs upon FFLs, eligible employees, or any State, local, or Tribal governmental entities. First, FFLs are not required by the rule to submit FHCs; FFLs may volunteer to submit FHCs. Similarly, FFLs will only incur minimal costs in terms of time and system upgrades if they opt to submit FHCs. Second, to submit an FHC, the eligible employee must have provided their informed, written consent for the background check. Agencies acting as “points of contact” (“POCs”) during NICS checks for firearm transfers will not be required to process FHCs unless they voluntarily choose to add FHC-related duties to their existing POC duties. POC duties are discussed further in Section II.A of this rule. Finally, this rule does not obligate State, local, and Tribal governmental entities to respond to FHC-related requests from the FBI or POCs.
Once effective, this rule will benefit FFLs that choose to submit FHCs by letting them know whether information available to NICS indicates the eligible employee is, or may be, prohibited from receiving or possessing firearms or ammunition. Having such information can assist FFLs in making informed determinations about whether that person should have employment duties that may involve access to firearms, ammunition, or their manufacturing components. This rule will also benefit public safety by implementing another mechanism that can keep more prohibited persons from being placed in positions that would otherwise afford them with access to firearms, ammunition, or their manufacturing components.
II. Background
A. Regulatory Context
BSCA made changes to Federal law regarding, among other things, firearms trafficking and the straw purchasing of firearms.
See
BSCA sec. 12004, 136 Stat. at 1326-1332. For instance, BSCA created new criminal offenses and increased punishments for some existing firearms-related offenses.
See id.
sec. 12004(a)(1), 136 Stat. at 1326-27 (
e.g.,
adding 18 U.S.C. 932 and 933). BSCA also provided for a new, voluntary use of NICS, requiring the Attorney General to promulgate regulations that will allow FFLs to access NICS “for purposes of voluntarily conducting an employment background
( printed page 67461)
check relating to a current or prospective employee.”
Id.
sec. 12004(h)(1)(B), 136 Stat. at 1330.
FFLs may inadvertently employ prohibited persons, who would then have access to firearms or ammunition through their employment duties and who may be able to use that access to engage in illegal firearms trafficking or straw purchases, or to otherwise illegally possess or use firearms. This rule's expanded authorization for FFLs to use NICS to conduct NICS checks regarding certain current or prospective FFL employees is an additional tool to help prevent those illegal actions by reducing opportunities that some prohibited persons might otherwise have had to gain access to firearms, ammunition, or their manufacturing components.
B. The System
1. NICS Procedure
The Brady Handgun Violence Prevention Act (“Brady Act”) required the Attorney General to establish NICS, which is a system that certain FFLs must contact before selling or otherwise transferring a firearm. Public Law 103-159, sec. 103, 107 Stat. 1536, 1541-43 (1993). Specifically, the Brady Act requires persons licensed by the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms, and Explosives (“ATF”) as manufacturers, dealers, or importers to initiate a NICS background check when seeking to transfer firearms to individuals who are not FFLs.
See18 U.S.C. 922(t)(1);
see also18 U.S.C. 921(a)(9)-(11) (defining “importer,” “manufacturer,” and “dealer”).[1]
NICS provides, when possible, immediate information on whether receipt or possession of a firearm by an unlicensed person would be prohibited.
See18 U.S.C. 922(t)(1). The FBI manages and operates NICS by delegation of the Attorney General pursuant to 28 CFR 25.3. The NICS Section of the FBI's Criminal Justice Information Services Division processed the first NICS background check on November 30, 1998.[2]
An FFL initiates a NICS background check by contacting the FBI's NICS Section [3]
or a State or local law enforcement agency known as a POC—
i.e.,
certain State or local law enforcement agencies with express or implied authority to perform NICS inquiries and respond to FFLs with the results.
See28 CFR 25.2, 25.6(a), (d).[4]
